title: Session log versioning — one integer, an upgrade chain, and a per-event ignorable marker
summary: The session log format has one integer version. A reader upgrades older logs through a chain of single-step upgraders, refuses newer logs with a message that names the direction, and may skip an unknown event only if that event is marked ignorable.
firstReason: The Go format is new, but it needs the same rules from its first release, because the refusal behaviour of the first shipped reader can never be added to copies already installed.

title: Handle-based session persistence
summary: Session persistence is five service methods (create, open, stat, list, flush) that return per-session handles with read, append, flush and close. Ownership is the handle, not a shared coordinator that adopts sessions by listening to events.
firstReason: Explicit handles make ownership and release clear and map naturally to a Go interface with a Close method; keep it.

title: Alpha Session migration refuses every unknown historical event
summary: The migration from the alpha v0 session format refuses any event type it does not know, even one marked ignorable, because a migration must prove that every payload it copies is still valid.
firstReason: The Go design does not read upstream session files, so there is no v0 format to migrate. The general lesson (a format migration refuses what it cannot validate) belongs to the versioning rules of the Go session format.

title: Released Session formats migrate through stateful streaming stages
summary: Old session formats are upgraded by streaming stages, one per version step, each holding only its own state. This replaced a whole-file migration that exhausted memory on a 116 MB session.
firstReason: The Go design starts at its own format version and has no upstream formats to migrate, but any future upgrade step must stream with bounded memory, which is the rule this decision establishes.

title: Historical Session reads prepare before write publication
summary: Opening an old-format session for reading waits only for the in-memory migration; writing the migrated file happens separately, and only a write open waits for it.
firstReason: There are no upstream formats to migrate in the Go design; the rule it should keep for its own future upgrades is that a read-only open never writes to storage or waits for publication.

title: Default DeepSeek Session-log upload
summary: Uploading the session log to the official DeepSeek API is on by default; setting enabled to false turns it off, the value is read for each request, and re-enabling sends whatever was not yet accepted.
firstReason: It is upstream's shipped product default and is carried over for parity; because it sends user data by default, the product owner should confirm the default for the Go design.

title: Record last activity in the session index
summary: Proposal (not built upstream): store the time of the last human prompt in the session index, so that listing stored sessions sorts correctly without opening each log or relying on an optional cache.
firstReason: Adopt the goal. Upstream left the storage shape open because its JSONL header cannot be rewritten; the Go format is new, so the session index can hold this value from the start.

title: Session historical data compatibility
summary: Proposal: the session refactor must not change stored bytes; old sessions keep opening after an upgrade, old generations are never overwritten, and search indexes are derived data that can be rebuilt.
firstReason: The promise to keep upstream's stored sessions readable does not apply, because the Go design does not read upstream session files. Its lasting rules (never overwrite an old generation, a derived index is never the recovery authority) are carried by the versioning and storage decisions.

title: Mandatory native V4 relationship validation
summary: Every read of a stored session runs one mandatory pass that checks relationships between events (turn and step order, tool calls and their results, retry chains, compaction spans, the protected system head) before the session is exposed. An unfinished tail may stay open, but a closing event must settle what it closes.
firstReason: An event can be well-formed by itself and still contradict earlier events; checking on read stops a damaged log from reaching the agent loop. The Go format needs the same single validation pass. The V3 and V4 history and the JavaScript prototype-property check do not carry over (DH-ADR-2).

title: Bounded DeepSeek Session-log upload
summary: The session-log upload attached to model requests is capped (8 MiB by default): each request carries the longest run of events after the acknowledged watermark that fits. An event too large to fit blocks the upload with a warning but never fails the model request.
firstReason: An unbounded first upload could exceed the JavaScript string limit and then fail on every retry. That limit is specific to the V8 engine, but an unbounded request body is a problem in any runtime, and the rule that an optional extension field must not fail the base request is worth keeping.

title: cross-process session write lease
summary: A session's write handle holds a kernel lock for its whole life: `flock` on a lock file on POSIX and a named kernel semaphore on Windows. The kernel releases it when the holder dies, so a crashed writer never blocks a successor and no expiry bookkeeping exists; a live but stuck holder keeps the lock until its process exits.
firstReason: Two processes appending to one log corrupt it, and only an arbiter outside every writer survives all failure modes. Go reaches the same kernel objects through system calls without a native add-on.

title: Session versions follow reader compatibility
summary: The session format version number changes only when existing readers would misread the new data. A change keeps the same version when older readers resume correctly, safely ignore an optional feature while preserving its records, or refuse a required feature before they execute, change or repair anything.
firstReason: The criterion (reader behaviour, not structural difference) is independent of the language and avoids a version bump and migration for every optional field. The Go session format should adopt it from its first release; "already released readers" then means released Go binaries.

title: JSONL-only first-party Session persistence
summary: The project owns and tests one authoritative physical session store. The storage contract stays neutral so that someone else could implement another backend, but a second first-party backend is not maintained. The full-text search index and the key-value store are separate, rebuildable or unrelated data.
firstReason: One authoritative store halves every contract, recovery and migration test matrix. The Go design should keep "one first-party store behind one interface"; which physical format that store uses is free under DH-ADR-2. Note that the note says the SQLite provider is absent, while the pinned checkout still contains `packages/session/session-persistence-sqlite`; the session area must settle which is current.

title: Fold the persistence interface into dsh-session
summary: Rejected proposal: move the storage contract and the shared write coordinator into the session package. Upstream keeps a separate contract package so that the boundary between session and storage backend stays clean.
firstReason: The goal of the rejection, a clean boundary between the session and its storage backends, still holds. The argument for a separate package does not transfer: upstream backends extend an abstract class and so must import the package that defines it, whereas a Go backend satisfies an interface without importing it. Package boundaries are free to change (DH-ADR-2), so the session area decides where the interface and the write coordinator live.

title: Truncate interrupted final turns on load
summary: Rejected proposal: on load, throw away everything after the last completed turn. Upstream instead keeps an interrupted final turn and closes it with synthetic records (error results for unanswered tool calls, a step end, and a turn end marked interrupted).
firstReason: The rejection still holds in Go. One turn can contain many steps and large tool output, and silently dropping it after a crash loses real work; the Go session must define the same repair, including what the synthetic records say.
